analysis.one_liner: Orders regulators to break up banks so large that their failure would threaten the economy.
analysis.headline: The bill was never voted on: introduced with no cosponsors in December 2018 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where it died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Financial Stability Oversight Council to flag any financial institution whose total exposure or total liability to U.S. persons reaches 3% or more of U.S. GDP as a "Too Big To Exist Institution." Once flagged, the Federal Reserve would supervise its restructuring, generally within two years, so it is no longer big enough to endanger the financial system. Flagged institutions would also lose access to Federal Reserve credit facilities and would be barred from funding speculative derivatives and hedging activity with insured deposits.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors, taxpayers, and the broader economy. When a bank is too big to fail, taxpayers and the FDIC insurance fund absorb the losses during a crisis, as happened in the 2008 bailouts. Forcing the largest banks to shrink reduces the chance of a taxpayer-funded rescue, protects insured deposits from being gambled on speculative derivatives, and makes the financial system easier to police.

how_it_helps.text: Any financial institution with total exposure equal to or greater than 3% of U.S. GDP can be designated a "Too Big To Exist Institution," and the Federal Reserve's Vice Chair for Supervision must supervise its restructuring within two years [S3].
A designated institution loses access to Federal Reserve credit facilities, including the discount window and any emergency lending, advances, or capital injections from federal institutions [S3].

A designated institution may not use insured deposits to fund speculative hedging, derivatives trading, or structured products like collateralized debt obligations, and may not conduct those activities in a way that puts insured deposits or the Deposit Insurance Fund at risk [S3].

The Federal Reserve and the Financial Stability Oversight Council must testify annually before the Senate Banking and House Financial Services Committees and submit an annual report on designations and restructuring, giving Congress ongoing oversight [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The largest Wall Street banks and other giant financial institutions — banks, insurers, and holding companies whose total liabilities to U.S. persons approach or exceed 3% of GDP. They would face forced divestiture or restructuring, loss of Fed backstop access, and restrictions on trading with insured deposits. Some customers of those megabanks might lose one-stop financial services, and industry groups argue scale brings efficiencies and stability.

drawbacks.text: The threshold — 3% of GDP for exposure or liabilities to U.S. persons — could sweep in insurers and other non-bank institutions, and the bill leaves the Council discretion to designate those in the 3–4% range, raising questions about consistency and predictability [S3].

Critics of breakup mandates argue that size alone is a crude measure of risk: a bank can be restructured to slip under the line without actually being safer, and forcing divestitures could be disruptive to credit markets during implementation. The bill delegates the key judgment to the Financial Stability Oversight Council and the Fed rather than fixing a definitive safe structure in law [S3].

Larger institutions argue the biggest banks also give U.S. companies access to global capital and that banning a designated institution from all Federal Reserve credit facilities could deepen a panic rather than calm it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — eliminating institutions too big to fail so taxpayers never again absorb banking losses — directly targets the structural problem behind the 2008 bailouts. The cost is borne by the affected firms and their shareholders, not by the general public. The main honest objection is design risk: the GDP-based threshold and the delegation to regulators could make outcomes depend on regulatory discretion, and firms might game the metric without becoming genuinely safer. On balance, the bill would impose real costs on a concentrated industry to reduce a risk that ordinary taxpayers and depositors currently carry.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 20, 2018 with zero cosponsors and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never acted on it; the 115th Congress ended two weeks later, killing the bill without a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Sherman introduced the Too Big To Fail, Too Big To Exist Act on December 20, 2018, in the final days of the 115th Congress [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day; no further action was recorded [S5].
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill was never reported out of committee or brought to the floor [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest financial institutions — banks and other firms whose exposure or liabilities to U.S. persons approach or exceed 3% of GDP — are better off, since they face no breakup mandate, no ban on Fed credit access, and no restrictions on using insured deposits for speculative trading. Taxpayers and depositors remain exposed to the too-big-to-fail risk the bill aimed to eliminate.

for.name: Rep. Brad Sherman
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-CA), bill sponsor; member of the House Financial Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 20, 2018 to require restructuring of financial institutions too big to fail

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; never considered the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on December 20, 2018 and took no action before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: With zero cosponsors, the bill had the backing of a single Democrat in a Republican-controlled 115th House, so it never had enough support to move.

industries.industry: The largest Wall Street banks and financial holding companies
industries.note: Firms with exposure or liabilities to U.S. persons at or above 3% of GDP would face mandatory supervised restructuring and a permanent ban on Federal Reserve credit access [S3]. Their size is what makes them able to demand taxpayer rescues in a crisis; breaking them up shifts that risk back onto their shareholders.

industries.industry: Big insurers and other non-bank financial institutions
industries.note: Covered by the designation scheme (with partial carve-outs for insurance claim liabilities and assets under management), so giant insurers could also be flagged and restructured [S3].

Designated institutions could no longer use insured deposits for speculative hedging, derivatives dealing, or structured products like CDOs and CLOs, shrinking a profitable trading business funded partly by federally insured money [S3].
